Mutations

Gene (point) mutations: base substitutions — transitions and transversions; by their consequences — silent, missense, nonsense; insertions and deletions — with or without a frameshift. Transitions are purine ↔ purine or pyrimidine ↔ pyrimidine, transversions are purine ↔ pyrimidine (HbS is an A → T transversion). There are also mutations in regulatory regions and splice sites (many β⁺-thalassemias). Chromosomal mutations — deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations; genomic mutations — a change in chromosome number (trisomy 21).

Causes and defenses

Replication errors, spontaneous deamination and depurination, UV light (thymine dimers), ionizing radiation, chemical mutagens. Repair: direct reversal, excision repair (base and nucleotide excision — a defect causes xeroderma pigmentosum), mismatch repair (defect — Lynch syndrome). See the “DNA” topic.

Post-translational modifications

  • Removal of methionine and the signal peptide, partial proteolysis.
  • Phosphorylation, acetylation (histones), methylation.
  • Glycosylation, lipid attachment (membrane anchors).
  • Hydroxylation (vitamin C), γ-carboxylation (vitamin K), disulfide bond formation.
  • Ubiquitination — degradation in the proteasome.

<b>Остаточный (небелковый) азот</b> — аз: Non-protein (residual) nitrogen is the nitrogen of everything left in the blood after the proteins are precipitated: about 14–28 mmol/L. Half of it is urea (made by the liver from ammonia); the rest is amino acids, uric acid (from purine breakdown), creatinine (from muscle creatine phosphate, produced at an almost constant rate) and a little ammonia. All of it is filtered in the renal glomerulus; urea and creatinine leave in the urine, while amino acids are almost completely and uric acid largely reabsorbed in the tubules. Creatinine and urea are the main markers of kidney function.

Non-protein nitrogen and acid–base balance

Blood non-protein (residual) nitrogen is 14–28 mmol/L: urea (~50%), amino acids (~25%), uric acid, creatine and creatinine, ammonia, bilirubin, indican. Azotemia can be retention azotemia (the kidneys fail to excrete) or production azotemia (too much is formed).

Blood buffer systems

  • Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃, pKₐ 6.1): ~55% of the blood’s buffer capacity; works together with the lungs and kidneys.
  • Hemoglobin (~35%): deoxyhemoglobin binds H⁺ — the Bohr effect.
  • Protein (plasma proteins); phosphate (HPO₄²⁻/H₂PO₄⁻, pKₐ 6.8) matters inside cells and in urine.

Kidneys

They reabsorb all the filtered HCO₃⁻ and generate new HCO₃⁻ by excreting H⁺ as titratable acids (phosphates) and as ammonium ions NH₄⁺ (from glutamine).
